# Preface {.unnumbered}

*Matthew Saponaro, Ph.D*

## About the Author

**Matthew Saponaro, Ph.D.**, earned his doctorate in Computer and Information Sciences from the University of Delaware. His research sits at the intersection of multi-agent systems, machine learning, and human movement — from adaptive, real-time coaching built on wearable sensor data, to computer-vision methods for gait and movement assessment, to using wearable video devices and drones to study how people use parks and recreational spaces. That same instinct — turning raw sensor, video, and activity data into insights people can actually act on — runs through this book.

This book grew out of his own lecture plans and course materials from the data science classes he has taught, shaped by years of classroom experience with exactly this age group.

*(This book's writing and editing were assisted by AI tools, used under the author's direction and review throughout.)*

## Why This Book Exists

Think about the last hour you spent on your phone. Every video your feed served you, every song your playlist queued up, every "players near you" match in your favorite game — none of it was random. Behind each of those moments, a computer looked at data about you (and millions of people like you) and made a prediction. Data science is the skill of understanding how those predictions get made — and learning to make them yourself.

That matters for two reasons. First, decisions about you are already being made with data: what content you see, what ads follow you around, even what colleges and employers might one day learn about you. Understanding how that works turns you from a passive target into an informed participant. Second, the ability to *question, filter, and reshape* data is a genuine superpower. Whether you end up in medicine, music, sports, gaming, or a career that doesn't exist yet, the people who can turn raw numbers into honest answers will be the ones others turn to.

The good news: you don't need to be a math genius or a seasoned programmer to start. You need curiosity and a willingness to ask good questions. This book supplies the rest.

## What This Book Covers

The book is organized into four units, each building on the last:

1.  **Unit I: Foundations** — what data actually is, how to work with it in spreadsheets, and how to turn it into visualizations that tell the truth.
2.  **Unit II: Programming for Data Science** — your introduction to Python and Pandas, the tools professionals use when a dataset (like Delaware's nearly 540,000 traffic crash records) is too big for a spreadsheet to handle.
3.  **Unit III: Understanding and Modeling Data** — statistics, ethics, machine learning, and modern AI: how computers find patterns, and how to judge whether those patterns can be trusted.
4.  **Unit IV: Communicating and Applying Data Science** — a capstone project and the art of data storytelling, because an insight nobody understands is an insight nobody uses.

Along the way you'll work with real datasets — traffic crashes, open government data, and information pulled live from the web — not toy examples invented for a textbook.

## Before You Dive In

Two short pages follow this one, and they're worth reading first. **How to Use This Book** explains the features you'll see in every chapter — callout boxes, code you can run yourself, and end-of-chapter roadmaps — and how to get the most out of them. **Using AI Responsibly** sets out how tools like ChatGPT and Claude fit into your learning: when they help you grow and when they quietly rob you of the skills you came here to build.

That's it. Turn the page, and let's start asking better questions of the data all around you.
